passage:
Tuesday
Dear Diary, I packed my bag for tomorrow before dinner: maths book, geometry box, the signed permission slip. Then I checked it again. Ma'am picked me to collect the class notebooks because "Aditi never forgets." That felt nice. But in the maths test I wrote 7 × 8 = 54 and only saw it after I handed it in. I kept thinking about it all through lunch. After school Joseph asked me to play catch and I said no, because of homework. He looked disappointed. I finished everything by five and then just sat on the bed. I think I could have played for half an hour. Tomorrow maybe I will.
Aditi

qa.q: What mistake did Aditi write in the maths test?
qa.a: Aditi wrote 7 × 8 = 54.

qa.q: What does thinking about the mistake all through lunch show about how Aditi feels?
qa.a: Aditi is worried by even a small error, and it keeps nagging long after the test.

qa.q: What choice does Aditi consider for tomorrow, and why might it help?
qa.a: Aditi thinks about playing for half an hour after homework, which would give rest and play some room back.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Aditi says no to catch again?
qa.a: He looked disappointed; he may feel left out or wonder whether Aditi still wants to play with him.

grounding: A child packs the bag early and finishes homework first, worries over a small mistake, earns the teacher's trust, and notices play getting squeezed out.

passage: In Farhan's house at the edge of the mustard fields, the school bag was packed every night before the lamp went out: slate, two notebooks, a pencil sharpened at both ends. His sister Alka laughed at him. "The school is ten minutes away." "What if the road floods?" he said. The teacher had made Farhan keeper of the library cupboard key, because he never lost anything. But on Saturday, when the boys shouted from the maidan for a cricket match, Farhan stayed on the charpai, rubbing out a letter he had written slightly crooked. Alka sat beside him. "The letter is fine. The match won't wait." He looked at the page, then at the field, and slowly closed the notebook.

qa.q: What was Farhan made keeper of?
qa.a: He was made keeper of the library cupboard key.

qa.q: What does rubbing out a slightly crooked letter suggest Farhan is worried about?
qa.a: He worries that even a tiny flaw makes his work wrong, so he keeps fixing it instead of going to play.

qa.q: What turning point came when Alka sat beside him?
qa.a: She told him the letter was fine and the match would not wait, and he chose to close the notebook.

qa.q: How does Alka see her brother's careful habits?
qa.a: She finds them a little funny and teases him, but she also sees play being squeezed out and nudges him toward the field.

grounding: A village boy packs his bag each night and is trusted for never losing things, but his worry over small mistakes crowds out play.

passage:
Sunday night. Tanvir packed his bag at eight, checked it, then checked it twice more. His sister Alka called from the lane, 'Cricket, one over!' 'Homework first,' he called back, though it was already done.
Wednesday. Mr. Rao made Tanvir monitor of the class library. 'You never forget anything,' he said. That evening Tanvir found one spelling mistake in his notebook and rewrote the whole page, his eyes stinging.
Saturday. It was Alka's birthday, and the cousins were playing hide-and-seek on the terrace. Tanvir stayed at his desk revising for a test that was still a week away. When he finally went up, the game was over. Alka looked at him. 'You missed my turn to seek,' she said quietly.

qa.q: What did Mr. Rao make Tanvir on Wednesday?
qa.a: Monitor of the class library.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he rewrote the whole page?
qa.a: He was anxious and upset, eyes stinging, as if one spelling mistake spoiled all his work.

qa.q: What small step could help Tanvir keep his care without losing play?
qa.a: Setting a finishing time for homework and then going out, and letting a small mistake be crossed out instead of rewriting whole pages.

qa.q: How does Alka feel when Tanvir misses her birthday game?
qa.a: Alka feels hurt and let down, telling him quietly that he missed her turn to seek.

grounding: Shows a diligent child who packs his bag early and worries over small mistakes, winning a teacher's trust while play gets squeezed out.

passage: Tanvir, checking your bag three times, you remind me of your Payal Nani at ten. In our school in Bikaner I packed my slate and books every night before I ate. Homework came before the well, before the swings, before anything. One ink blot and I'd copy the whole page again, crying. Masterji noticed. He gave me the key to the chalk cupboard, the only child he trusted with it, and I wore it on a string like gold. But that Teej, all my friends were on the swings and I sat inside doing sums nobody had set. My father stood in the doorway. 'Payal, the sums will wait. The swing won't.' I went. Next day my work was just as good.

qa.q: What did Masterji give Payal?
qa.a: The key to the chalk cupboard.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she copied a whole page after one ink blot?
qa.a: She was anxious and upset, crying, because one small mistake felt unbearable.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Payal rest, and what did she find?
qa.a: Her father telling her the sums would wait but the swing wouldn't; she went, and her work the next day was just as good.

qa.q: How might Masterji have seen Payal?
qa.a: He saw her as the most reliable child, trusting her alone with the chalk cupboard key.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a diligent child whose carefulness wins a teacher's trust but squeezes out play, until a parent encourages rest.

passage: The power went out at eight, and Imran's bag was only half packed. He found the candle under the sink and set it on his desk. Maths notebook, English reader, geometry box. The geometry box. Not there. His stomach dropped. Tomorrow was the unit test, and Mrs. Dsouza always said Imran was the one she never had to remind. Outside, Divyansh banged on the window. 'Come! The lane's flooded, we're floating paper boats!' 'Can't. Packing.' Imran searched under the bed, behind the cupboard, inside his school shoes. At half past nine he found it in yesterday's lunch bag. He checked the bag twice more by candlelight, while outside the laughing faded away.

qa.q: Where did Imran finally find the geometry box?
qa.a: In yesterday's lunch bag.

qa.q: Why did Imran's stomach drop when the geometry box wasn't there?
qa.a: He was anxious about arriving unprepared for the test and letting down Mrs. Dsouza, who trusted him never to need a reminder.

qa.q: Once the box was found, what could Imran have done instead?
qa.a: Checked the bag once and then gone out to float boats with Divyansh for a while, letting himself rest.

qa.q: What might Divyansh think of Imran staying in?
qa.a: Divyansh might be disappointed or puzzled that Imran chose packing over the flooded lane, and miss Imran's company.

grounding: Shows a diligent child who packs the night before and worries over a small missing item, earning a teacher's trust while play is squeezed out.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Aparna, ten, packed her school bag every night before dinner: books in timetable order, pencils sharpened, water bottle filled. On Saraswati Puja week, while the colony children rehearsed their dance, she stayed home to finish her homework first. When she crossed out one word in her essay, she tore out the page and started again, worried it looked messy. Her teacher, Manjula Ma'am, made her class monitor because she never forgot anything. But at break one day, Manjula noticed Aparna sitting inside, revising again. "Aparna, the monitor gets a break too. Go and play for ten minutes." Aparna hesitated, then ran out. She came back pink-cheeked and laughing.

qa.q: What did Aparna pack every night before dinner?
qa.a: Her school bag: books in timetable order, pencils sharpened, water bottle filled.

qa.q: Why did Aparna tear out the essay page?
qa.a: She felt worried and uneasy that one crossed-out word made it look messy.

qa.q: What did Manjula Ma'am do that was wise?
qa.a: She trusted Aparna's reliability as monitor but also noticed her missing play and sent her out for a break.

qa.q: How might Manjula Ma'am see Aparna?
qa.a: She sees her as reliable and trustworthy, but also as a child who needs rest and play.

grounding: Shows a diligent child who packs her bag early, finishes homework first and worries about small mistakes, trusted by her teacher though play gets squeezed out.
